title: Discovering Opinion Intervals from Conflicts in Signed Graphs

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 2.2, Section 2.1, Appendix A, and all downstream hardness claims
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The stated theorem explicitly retracts the reduction: “the proposed reduction does not guarantee an equivalence between acyclic partitions and conflict-free interval representations in G. Therefore, the NP-hardness claim ... remains open.” Nevertheless, the immediately following text asserts consequences of a hardness result, the appendix presents the invalid construction as a completed proof, and the conclusion says “We gave strong hardness results for incomplete graphs.” These claims cannot simultaneously be true. The NP-hardness theorem, inapproximability claim, and parameterized-hardness consequences must be removed or replaced by a corrected proof.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.1, paragraph beginning “The theorem has several implications...”, claim that forbidden induced subgraphs are NP-hard to detect
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states that its hardness result “implies that detecting these forbidden structures is NP-hard for incomplete signed graphs.” This does not follow and is false as written. Given the positive graph G+ explicitly, testing whether it is an interval graph and detecting a forbidden induced subgraph can be done in polynomial time by interval-graph recognition algorithms; indeed the cited interval-graph-recognition literature concerns precisely this. The signed-graph optimization problem may be difficult, but that is not equivalent to detecting forbidden induced subgraphs of G+.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 2.3, first paragraph in Appendix B
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof says it can enumerate all 2^{binom(k,2)} pairwise overlap patterns of k intervals and optimize over them. Most binary overlap patterns are not realizable as intersection graphs of intervals. For example, an induced cycle C4 is not an interval graph, so no four intervals have exactly that overlap pattern. The proposed enumeration includes such non-realizable patterns, and Algorithm 2 can select an assignment under an invalid pattern, which is not a feasible BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION solution. The proof must restrict enumeration to realizable interval-overlap graphs and show how to construct corresponding intervals.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.2, paragraph after the overview of the claimed PTAS
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper claims Theorem 2.3 as a PTAS for complete graphs with fixed k, but then says: “overlapping intervals introduce intricate dependencies making greedy assignments approximate at best” and “while a PTAS is feasible for limited and well-structured interval overlaps, the general case requires further algorithmic innovations beyond current methods.” This directly undercuts the theorem’s claimed generality. No definition is given for the supposedly restricted “limited and well-structured” class, nor is Theorem 2.3 restricted to it. The theorem statement, proof, and this disclaimer must be reconciled.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix C.2, discussion immediately following Table 3
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text says “WikiConflict [is] the only dataset with more than 1% improvement” beyond 8-Chains. Table 3 contradicts this for BitcoinOTC under VENUS: the best disagreement falls from 760 with an 8-Chain to 716 with a 16-Chain, a reduction of 44/760 = 5.8%. Thus the stated empirical summary is false under the natural relative-improvement interpretation used elsewhere in the paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4, RQ4 interpretability discussion and Appendix C.7 Bundestag case study
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper claims that the aggregate 2012–2025 co-voting embedding “reveals the coalition governments throughout the past decade” and attributes party splitting to coalition history. The experiment is a single aggregate signed graph with no temporal model, no coalition labels used for validation, no statistical test, and party affiliation for visualization is assigned using the first affiliation even for politicians who changed parties. The data show an association in one heuristic solution, not evidence that the inferred intervals reveal or identify historical coalitions. The paper itself later concedes that “temporal effects might drive this structure” and that robustness is uncertain.

predicted_errors.error_location: Second occurrence of Section 5 Conclusion, after Figure 4
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: After a complete conclusion, the document contains a second “Conclusion” heading beginning mid-sentence: “instances, and it is tight, for instance, when taking two cliques...” The antecedent and preceding result are absent. This is not a coherent conclusion section and appears to be a truncated or misplaced fragment; it prevents readers from determining what bound or statement is claimed to be tight.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract, Introduction ‘Our results,’ Related Work, and Conclusion
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Several portions retain incompatible editorial states. The abstract describes only “preliminary hardness results” and says guarantees remain open; Theorem 2.2 explicitly says hardness is open; yet the introduction, appendix, and conclusion repeatedly present a completed NP-hardness proof and “strong hardness results.” These are not merely different levels of caution: they make mutually incompatible claims about whether the central theorem has been established.
